summary: Specifies the extensions a host's IP implementation needs to support multicasting, delivering a datagram to a host group identified by a single address. Delivery is best-effort, like unicast. It is a major revision of RFC 988, and was replaced by RFC 1112.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of sending the same letter to each friend, you send one letter to a club address and everyone who joined gets a copy.

subtitle: How IP hosts send messages to groups of computers simultaneously.

tldr.problem: Some applications need to send a message to multiple computers at the same time, but unicast (one-to-one) IP datagrams reach only a single destination.
tldr.mechanism: IP multicasting allows a host to send a single datagram to a special multicast address, and all hosts that have joined that group receive a copy delivered with best-effort reliability.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now reach groups of computers efficiently without sending duplicate messages. This was a major revision of RFC 988 and was replaced by RFC 1112.

today: RFC 1054 was obsoleted by RFC 1112, which is the current specification for IP multicast host extensions. The concepts introduced in this RFC remain fundamental to multicast IP networking today.

sections.title: What IP Multicasting Does
sections.content:
IP multicasting allows a single IP datagram to be sent to a host group, a set of zero or more computers identified by one multicast address. All members of the group receive a copy of the datagram with the same best-effort reliability as regular unicast IP datagrams: it may be lost, may arrive out of order, or may never reach some group members.

Host group membership is dynamic. Computers can join or leave groups at any time, and there is no restriction on how many members a group can have. A single computer can be a member of multiple groups simultaneously. Importantly, a computer does not need to be a member of a group to send datagrams to it.

Groups can be permanent (with a well-known, administratively assigned address) or transient (created on demand for as long as they have members). Multicast routers forward datagrams from one network to another, allowing groups to span the entire internetwork.
sections.plainLanguage: A multicast group is like a public club. Anyone can send mail to the club address, and all club members automatically get a copy. Members can join or leave anytime.

sections.title: Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
Host groups are identified using class D IP addresses, which have the binary pattern 1110 in their four highest-order bits. In dotted-decimal notation, multicast addresses range from 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255. The address 224.0.0.0 is reserved and never assigned, while 224.0.0.1 is the permanent group of all IP hosts on the local network.

The address space is divided into permanent groups (assigned by network administrators and published in Assigned Numbers) and transient groups (dynamically allocated and used temporarily). Since there are 28 significant bits available for multicast group addresses, there is plenty of address space for both purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast addresses start with 224 through 239 in the first number. 224.0.0.1 means all computers on your local network, and other addresses identify different clubs.

sections.title: Three Levels of Support
sections.content:
This RFC defines three levels of conformance to IP multicasting. Level 0 means the host does not support multicasting at all and simply discards any multicast datagrams it receives (recognized by class D destination addresses). Level 1 hosts can send multicast datagrams but cannot join groups to receive them, suitable for applications like resource discovery or status reporting. Level 2 hosts support full multicasting: they can join and leave host groups and both send and receive multicast datagrams.

Level 2 implementations require the Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) for coordination with multicast routers. Full support involves extensions to the IP module and local network interfaces to handle multicast addresses and group membership.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers ignore multicasts entirely, some can send club mail but not read it, and the most capable ones can send and receive club mail and manage their group memberships.

sections.title: How Multicasting Works on Networks
sections.content:
When a host sends a multicast datagram, it is transmitted as a local network multicast that reaches all immediately neighboring members of the destination group. If the datagram's time-to-live (TTL) is greater than 1, multicast routers on the local network forward it toward other networks that have members of that group. On those networks, a multicast router completes delivery by transmitting the datagram as a local multicast.

For Ethernet networks, IP multicast addresses are mapped to Ethernet multicast addresses by placing the low-order 23 bits of the IP multicast address into the Ethernet multicast address 01-00-5E-00-00-00 (hex). Other network types handle the mapping differently depending on their capabilities: networks that support native multicasting use a similar approach, broadcast-only networks may map all multicast addresses to a single broadcast address, and point-to-point links transmit multicasts like regular unicasts.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send a club letter, your local post office delivers it to all club members nearby. If the letter says it can travel far, post offices in distant places also deliver copies to their club members.

sections.title: Joining and Leaving Groups
sections.content:
Level 2 hosts use two operations to manage group membership: JoinHostGroup (which specifies a multicast address and network interface) and LeaveHostGroup (which removes membership). These are non-blocking operations that return immediately with success or failure. Multiple upper-layer protocols on the same host can request membership in the same group, and membership persists as long as at least one protocol is joined.

The local network module is notified only when the first join or last leave happens on a given interface, so it can update its multicast reception filter to efficiently receive only packets destined to groups the host actually wants. The IP module maintains a list of group memberships for each network interface and delivers incoming multicast datagrams to all upper-layer protocols that have joined the destination group.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers tell their local post office which clubs they are joining or leaving so mail gets delivered to the right mailboxes.
